transcript.text: Hello, I'm Dikum Sheyam, Research Aerospace Engineer.
Here at the NASA Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio,
we've been researching and developing innovative aeronautics
and space technologies for almost eight decades.
During the 2018 to 2019 academic year,
NASA Glenn would like you to join our third space-themed
university student design challenge.
Imagine joining a future team of investigators,
living in a habitat far, far away from Earth,
in the clouds of Venus.
Your team is exploring the idea that some life on Earth
may have originated on Venus, a fiery planet
with surface temperatures hot enough to melt
the atmosphere of sulfuric acid and surface air
pressures high enough to crush a submarine in minutes.
Could a runaway greenhouse effect
have evaporated the planet's water?
Could that have swept bacteria or spores up
into the planet's upper atmosphere
and then on into interstellar space?
By looking for evidence of microbial Venusian life,
you will also be terraforming Venus for human habitation.
Will you be doing this from a bio-inspired Earth-independent
platform floating high in the Venusian sky?
What does this platform look like?
Does it use wind power, solar power?
How does the Venusian day, which is longer than the planets
here, affect the theme's work and the platform's power systems?
How will you protect the platform from the corrosive atmosphere
and high winds?
Are you up to the challenge?
NASA's University Student Design Space Challenge gives teams
a full-time junior and senior undergraduate students
the opportunity to work with top NASA experts
in designing a bio-inspired mission
to create an off-world habitat to test the pan-spermia hypothesis.
Your team should look at natural models like bugs, plants,
and bio-nekinisms for fluid transports such as tree roots
and translate those into mechanical systems.
If you're using photovoltaic systems, for example,
you may wish to look at the ways nature concentrates life
or how plants or other organisms convert photons
into chemical energy.
Is there a way to use Venus' toxic atmospheric gases
to create water?
Can looking at how organisms store food
or what shapes they use to build help you to design
a stronger, more resilient habitat or surface vehicles
that can withstand severe heat and atmospheric pressures?
Will you be working on the surface of Venus
or from a platform floating in the Venusian sky?
What will your platform look like?
How is it powered?
How does the Venusian day affect the platform's performance
and its power systems and maintenance crew?
People on your team will obviously come from science,
technology, engineering, and mathematics backgrounds.
But you'll also want to include individuals from economics,
marketing, graphic arts, and other areas
to help strengthen your project concept.
This may result in a better and more feasible design.
Your team will compete against other college teams
under the supervision of a college advisor.
An expert from NASA Glenn Research Center
will mentor your team as it immerses itself
in NASA-related research from space scientists,
physicists, chemists, engineers, and power systems experts.
For a complete list of project requirements,
be sure to attend the mandatory virtual space project
kickoff meeting in November.
You can also visit us on the web.
I look forward to seeing your team's
bio-inspired Venus habitat.
Thanks for being part of the NASA team and good luck.
